lesson.title: Aiming for the Bullseye: What Makes an Estimator Unbiased
lesson.summary: An estimator is unbiased when the mean of its sampling distribution equals the true value of the population parameter it is trying to estimate, so it does not systematically run high or low.
lesson.body:
Recall that a parameter is a fixed number describing a population (like the true proportion of voters who support a candidate, or the true mean height of every giraffe on a reserve), and a statistic is a number computed from a sample that is used to estimate that parameter. Because a sample only ever captures part of the population, a statistic will almost never equal the parameter exactly. Different samples give different statistics, and the collection of all those possible values, weighted by how likely each sample is to occur, is the sampling distribution. The question this chapter asks is: does the sampling distribution, taken as a whole, aim at the right target?

An estimator is called unbiased if the mean of its sampling distribution is exactly equal to the parameter it estimates. This does not mean any single sample gives the exact right answer, it means that if you repeated the sampling process over and over, forever, and averaged all the resulting statistics together, that average would land exactly on the parameter. Bias is not about how spread out the sampling distribution is, only about where it is centered.

A target-shooting analogy helps. Imagine an archer whose arrows scatter widely around the bullseye but are centered on it: individual shots miss, sometimes by a lot, but there is no consistent pull to one side. That archer is unbiased even though far from precise. Now imagine an archer whose arrows land in a tight cluster, but that cluster is consistently three inches to the left of the bullseye. That archer is precise but biased. Unbiasedness describes centering, not consistency.

A small numeric example makes this concrete. Suppose a tiny population contains exactly three values: 1, 2, and 3, so the population mean, mu, is (1 + 2 + 3) / 3 = 2. Now suppose we sample two of these three values without replacement and compute the sample mean each time. There are three possible samples: {1, 2} with mean 1.5, {1, 3} with mean 2, and {2, 3} with mean 2.5. Averaging these three possible sample means gives (1.5 + 2 + 2.5) / 3 = 6 / 3 = 2, which is exactly mu. The sampling distribution of the sample mean is centered exactly on the population mean, so in this small world, the sample mean behaved as an unbiased estimator.

This idea matters because it tells us which statistics are trustworthy targets to aim at in the long run. Later in this unit we will show formally that the sample proportion is an unbiased estimator of the population proportion, and the sample mean is an unbiased estimator of the population mean. Not every statistic earns that label, and the next chapter looks at what happens when a statistic systematically misses.
